title: Joseph weeps
hook: Joseph reveals himself to the brothers who sold him, and weeps (Genesis 45:1–15)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Mishnah's rule for wrongs against people: ask them first. Did you say the plain words? Today, the other side of the table: a man who was wronged, and his brothers standing in front of him. Day nine hundred forty-three.

Egypt. A room in the governor's house. The brothers from Canaan stand before the governor of Egypt, and they're terrified. A silver cup was found in the sack of the youngest, Benjamin, and now the governor means to keep him as a slave. Judah steps forward and offers himself instead. He can't go home without the boy, he says; it would kill their old father. What the brothers don't know is that the governor understands every word. He is Joseph, the brother they sold into slavery years ago. And he has just reached the end of what he can hold in.
screen: `A ROOM IN EGYPT.` → `JUDAH OFFERS HIMSELF.` → `THE GOVERNOR IS JOSEPH.`

segments.voice: First, the room empties. In the King James words: "Then Joseph could not refrain himself before all them that stood by him; and he cried, Cause every man to go out from me." He sends the Egyptians out. Whatever happens next, he won't make his brothers face it in front of strangers. Second, the sound. "And he wept aloud: and the Egyptians and the house of Pharaoh heard." This isn't the first time. Earlier in the story he turned away from them to weep, and once he hurried out to find a private room. This time there's nowhere to hide it, and he doesn't try. Then the words, as plain as they could be: "I am Joseph your brother, whom ye sold into Egypt." He names exactly what they did. Third, what he does with it. The brothers can't answer. So Joseph keeps talking: don't be grieved, he tells them, nor angry with yourselves, and he says God sent him ahead to keep people alive through the famine. Readers disagree about this. Some hear deep forgiveness. Some notice he never says the words I forgive you, and that later in Genesis, after their father dies, the brothers are afraid all over again. The text lets both readings stand. Fourth, the last line. Joseph kisses each of them and weeps on them. Then the text says: "and after that his brethren talked with him." After the tears, talking. It's a small phrase, and it may be the whole point. Years of silence, and then a family in one room, speaking again.
screen: `CAUSE EVERY MAN TO GO OUT.` · `HE WEPT ALOUD.` · `I AM JOSEPH YOUR BROTHER.` · `AFTER THAT, THEY TALKED.` · then, large: `HE WEPT ALOUD.`

segments.voice: Let the breath find its own pace. Bring to mind someone who hurt you, and choose someone where the hurt is real but not the deepest one. Let their face come. Notice whatever rises when it does, in the hands or the stomach or the breath. You don't have to push it away. Just let it soften by one degree. Breathe out, and let the shoulders drop a little. You're not saying it was fine. Like Joseph, you can name exactly what happened and still let something loosen. If you pray, you can hold that person in your prayer, just as they are. The bell holds the time.
Joseph weeps. Face to face with the brothers who sold him, Joseph sends the room out, weeps aloud, and names who he is. Today's word.
Your line: he wept aloud. Today, when you think of the person you chose, let your shoulders drop one degree, and notice what changes. Day nine hundred forty-three.

howItsDone: Jews read the story of Joseph and his brothers in the weekly Torah portions in synagogue, and Christians read it in Genesis too; it is often taught as a story of reconciliation within a family.

fork.setup: you're Joseph. the brothers who sold you stand before you, not knowing who you are. Judah has just offered himself as a slave for Benjamin. what do you do?
options: send everyone out and tell them who you are.
fork.reveal: Joseph can't hold it in: he sends every man out, weeps aloud so the house of Pharaoh hears, and says, "I am Joseph your brother."

trapdoor: what you thought: a happy reunion in an old story.
what it means: a wronged brother names the wrong plainly, weeps, and opens the way to talk again.
what a scholar hears: readers differ on whether Genesis 45 is forgiveness at all: Joseph never says I forgive you, and in Genesis 50 the brothers fear him again after Jacob dies.

notes: 'Sold into slavery years ago': no number of years given deliberately.
Earlier weeping: Genesis 42:24 (turned himself about and wept) and 43:30 (sought where to weep; entered his chamber). Paraphrased.
The debate over whether Genesis 45 is forgiveness, and the brothers' fear in Genesis 50:15–21, are attributed to 'readers'. Day 943 avoids teaching Genesis 50 at length in case a later day takes it.
